title: Quantization technical review - Aurora Solutions
next_steps: Send GPTQ vs AWQ benchmark spreadsheet and notes
Run FP8 evaluation on Aurora eval set and share results
Schedule on-prem/VPC deployment planning session w/ infra team
action_items: Daniel Ortiz: run quantized benchmarks (GPTQ/AWQ/INT8/FP8) on Aurora workloads - due 2027-09-28
Maya Chen: send SOC2/security docs and pricing for Dedicated/Private options - due 2027-09-23
Priya Kapoor: provide 500 eval prompts + sample data access for accuracy checks - due 2027-09-24
summary: Redwood SEs walked Aurora through INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ tradeoffs and runtime performance implications. Primary concerns were accuracy regressions on domain prompts, KV cache behavior with quantized weights, and networking constraints for VPC/on-prem. Agreed next steps to run customer-specific benchmarks and plan a deployment workshop.
transcript: 00:00 Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for hopping on, i'm maya from Redwood, i'll kick us off. we have daniel and lena from our se team too.
00:12 Priya Kapoor: hi thanks, we've got liam and sofia on our side, excited to dig into quantization tradeoffs, we've seen mixed results with int8 in prod.
00:27 Daniel Ortiz: great yeah, high level today we'll cover gptq vs awq, int8 vs fp8, runtime impacts, and some notes about kv cache and batching when you quantize.

00:44 Liam O'Neill: quick note on infra - Aurora is planning a VPC private deployment, possibly on-prem later, so network and KMS are important, and we need to know if quantized models change cache behavior.
01:02 Lena Park: yeah the K V cache interactions are interesting, we've seen some customers see higher latency on cache misses with certain kernels, we'll show our benchmarks.
01:18 Sofia Martinez: also curious about hallucination increases after gptq, and whether awq helps preserve fp32 accuracy more consistently.

01:33 Daniel Ortiz: absolutely. to set expectations, gptq usually gives smaller model sizes but can have spillover accuracy regressions on narrow domain prompts; awq was designed to mitigate some of that by grouping quantization differently.
01:53 Maya Chen: we'll share a spreadsheet with our across-model results, but we'll also run Aurora-specific runs once you share the prompts.
02:08 Priya Kapoor: yes will do, we can get the eval set over after the call. timeline wise we'd like a pilot by early october if possible.
02:20 Daniel Ortiz: that's doable; depends on dataset size and the hardware profile. speaking of, what hardware are you planning for private?
02:35 Liam O'Neill: initially g4-ish equivalence in our colo, but long term we can target a mix of A100-like and integer-optimized infer nodes, maybe smaller ampere type GPUs.
02:50 Daniel Ortiz: ok good to know. for int8, hardware and kernel selection matter a lot — some runtimes use per-channel scales which helps, others do per-tensor which hurts accuracy.
03:06 Sofia Martinez: can you explain the fp8 claim? we've heard fp8 can keep accuracy but at what perf cost?

03:18 Lena Park: fp8 (we've seen both e4m and other fp8 formats) tends to preserve outliers better vs straight int8. performance-wise, on some kernels fp8 can be slightly slower per-token than int8 but faster than fp16 in batched throughput for some models because it reduces memory bandwidth.

03:42 Daniel Ortiz: right, and with fp8 you still need quantization calibration; post-training quantization vs qat matters but we typically do post-training for inference. awq and gptq are different — gptq is weight-only quant that reconstructs Hessian info in some variants; awq uses groupwise schemes.
04:02 Priya Kapoor: we've got strong domain-specific tokens, legal docs, so small accuracy drops are big deal for us. how do you measure regression risk?

04:16 Daniel Ortiz: we run both scalar metrics like exact match and ppl on held-out domain prompts and also human evals on a sample set; we also track per-prompt deltas and worst-case percentiles, because average can hide edge cases.

04:38 Maya Chen: also re: KV cache, one thing to watch is quantization-induced misalignment of cache addressing on some runtimes — you'll see slightly different cache hit patterns when the runtime switches kernels mid-context.
04:58 Liam O'Neill: misalignment meaning what exactly? does the cache get invalidated?

05:08 Daniel Ortiz: not invalidated, but the effective representation of key/values changes and some runtimes allocate different sizes for kv chunks under certain quant kernels, which can increase latency on first continued token generation for long contexts.
05:28 Sofia Martinez: so prefix caching could be less effective? we've optimized around it heavily.

05:36 Lena Park: prefix caching still helps a ton, but you might see slightly higher initial token latency on cache warmup; overall throughput tends to be better though because of reduced memory IO per token when quantized.
06:00 Priya Kapoor: what's your recommendation for batching vs latency? our product requires sub-200ms tail P99 on short chat flows.

06:12 Daniel Ortiz: for strict tail latency you want small batch sizes and low batching windows; quantization helps reduce per-token compute but batching policy is still key. we offer auto-batching that respects latency SLOs and will fall back to a lower-quant model for spikes.
06:33 Liam O'Neill: is fallback automated? we don't want silent quality drops for certain tenants.
06:40 Maya Chen: fallbacks are policy-driven and visible in the console; you can set route-level policies to prefer higher-precision models for certain customers or PII routes.

07:00 Daniel Ortiz: jumping back to accuracy, here's an example: we ran gptq-int8 for a 7B model and saw mean token accuracy drop 1.8% but worst-case prompt delta of 12% on legal clauses. AWQ reduced worst-case to 5% at slightly higher size.
07:25 Priya Kapoor: that worst-case is our fear. can you tune gptq to reduce that?

07:32 Daniel Ortiz: sometimes fine-tuning a small calibration set or hybrid quant where critical layers stay fp16 helps; we often keep attention and first/last MLP in higher precision (mixed quant) to preserve semantics.
07:54 Sofia Martinez: how many layers do you normally keep at higher precision?

08:00 Lena Park: common pattern is keep the first two layers and the final output layer at fp16, maybe attention q/k/v in fp16 for sensitive tasks. it's model-dependent; we automate a sweep to find minimal high-precision layers.
08:20 Priya Kapoor: any latency numbers you can share? for 7B on A100-ish, quantized throughput vs fp16?

08:30 Daniel Ortiz: roughly, int8 GPTQ can give 1.8–2.4x throughput vs fp16 in our bench on throughput-heavy runs; fp8 sits around 1.4–1.9x depending on kernel and sequence length. tail latency for single-stream low-batch can improve but is more modest like 10–30%.
08:58 Liam O'Neill: sequence length matters because kv cache size changes, right?
09:05 Daniel Ortiz: exactly — longer contexts amplify memory-bandwidth savings from quantization. one caveat: some implementations have to transcode kv shards on the fly which can spike CPU usage.
09:22 Priya Kapoor: you mentioned kernel selection earlier. how does Redwood pick kernels for awq/gptq on different hardware?

09:30 Lena Park: our compilation layer profiles the model and workload distribution; it chooses kernels tuned for sequence length and attention patterns, and we have fallbacks. if a kernel exhibits accuracy regressions on your eval set, we can force an alternate kernel.
09:49 Sofia Martinez: we ran a few back-to-back on-prem tests and saw inconsistent numbers — maybe we were hitting different kernels due to batch variance.
10:00 Daniel Ortiz: that could be it; we also track telemetry per-route so we can correlate kernel changes with metric shifts.
10:15 Priya Kapoor: about VPC / on-prem: are there any limitations to running quantized runtimes privately?

10:24 Maya Chen: no functional limitations, but you need to ensure the private control plane can pull optimized kernels or we provide a signed artifact. also KMS for key unwrapping is required if you use encrypted model artifacts.
10:40 Liam O'Neill: model artifact signing, okay. does that change when using AWQ vs GPTQ?

10:48 Lena Park: not really — it's orthogonal. it's about how you deliver the runtime + kernels; quantized weights are just different model weights. audit logs and SBOM are provided for Private deployments.
11:05 Priya Kapoor: any guidance on model rollout strategies to catch regressions early?

11:12 Daniel Ortiz: canary on a small percent of traffic with route-level evaluation sets, offline regression detection per-prompt, and automatic rollback on metric breaches. Redwood Console supports A/B with automatic fallback.
11:30 Sofia Martinez: for our acceptance criteria we'd want PPL delta < 0.5 and no more than 2% of prompts with >10% semantic delta, is that realistic?
11:42 Daniel Ortiz: it's aggressive but achievable for many models with AWQ or mixed-precision hybrid; GPTQ might need more careful tuning or leaving more layers at fp16.
12:00 Maya Chen: we'll run the acceptance criteria tests once you send the prompts and share a validation harness that you can run in your environment.
12:12 Priya Kapoor: quick Q on tooling — can we run Redwood Optimize's batching suggestions locally?
12:20 Lena Park: yes, we provide a lightweight profiler that you can run in private to collect timing and sequence distribution, then our service suggests batching windows and kv cache parameters.
12:36 Liam O'Neill: any CPU implications for transcoding or dequantization during generation? we have limited CPU headroom in our colo nodes.

12:46 Daniel Ortiz: some runtimes do CPU dequant when assembling kv, but Redwood's runtime keeps most of that on GPU where possible. there can be CPU spikes during model load or when converting attention caches across kernels.
13:02 Sofia Martinez: what about model size on disk and network transfer for private deploys? int8/gptq reduces artifact size a lot, fp8 less so but still smaller than fp16.
13:12 Lena Park: yes int8 artifacts can be ~2-4x smaller vs fp16 depending on format, which helps network transfer and cold start times.
13:26 Priya Kapoor: okay good. i'd like to understand the human eval workflow you mentioned — how long does that take?
13:34 Daniel Ortiz: we usually run an automated pass then a human eval on 200-500 prompts which takes 2-4 business days depending on availability; for critical legal prompts we suggest more sampling.
13:50 Maya Chen: we'll estimate timeline for the pilot after today's bench run is scheduled. next steps we'll share the benchmark template and run on our side and yours.
14:02 Priya Kapoor: sounds good. can you walk us through an example benchmark result?

14:08 Daniel Ortiz: sure — here's a common result slide: fp16 baseline, gptq-int8 reduces latency 45%, throughput up 2.0x, mean ppl delta 0.5, but worst-case prompt delta 10-15% for legal wording. awq-int8 reduces worst-case to ~4-7% and throughput 1.7x.
14:38 Sofia Martinez: do you have automated diagnostics to point to which layers cause worst-case deltas?
14:46 Lena Park: yes we run layer-wise sensitivity where we quantize one layer at a time and measure the delta; that gives a heatmap to decide mixed-precision config.
15:00 Liam O'Neill: any recommendations on monitoring in prod for these regressions?
15:06 Daniel Ortiz: route-level eval sets, drift monitoring on token distributions, and occasionally sample human checks. also set alerting on sudden PPL or exact-match drops.
15:20 Priya Kapoor: ok that's helpful. one more question: how mature is FP8 on common clouds?

15:28 Lena Park: FP8 support is growing; some cloud vendors provide optimized fp8 kernels, others rely on custom runtime kernels. for Private we'd ship optimized kernels validated against your hardware.
15:42 Sofia Martinez: awesome. can we get a sample of the kernel telemetry you mentioned?
15:48 Daniel Ortiz: yes we'll attach an example telemetry dump and mapping doc showing kernel-to-behavior, but it's somewhat technical.
16:00 Maya Chen: to recap — action items are daniel runs benchmarks, maya sends security/pricing, priya shares prompts. we'll aim to have pilot plan by next week.
16:16 Priya Kapoor: thanks everyone, looking forward to the results. we'll schedule the deployment workshop once bench look good.
16:26 Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the spreadsheet. bye.
55:00 <meeting end>
